subject: Biotechnology
title: Cell-Free Protein Synthesis
description: A short lesson to help you apply Cell-Free Protein Synthesis.

hook.text: Skip the cell entirely — cell-free systems produce proteins in a test tube using just the molecular machinery.

buildup.text: Cell extract contains ribosomes, tRNA, and energy molecules — add DNA template and protein appears in hours.

discovery.text: Toxic proteins that kill cells can be made cell-free — no living host means no viability constraints.

twist.text: Cell-free systems are freeze-dried and shipped — just add water to activate protein production anywhere.

climax.text: Field diagnostics for Zika and Ebola use freeze-dried cell-free reactions on paper — lab accuracy without the lab.

punchline.text: Biology without cells — cell-free systems are biology's instant mix.

quiz.question: What advantage does cell-free synthesis have for making toxic proteins?
options: Toxic proteins become non-toxic in cell-free reactions
No living cell needs to survive, so proteins that would kill cells can be produced freely
Cell-free systems automatically neutralize toxic protein effects

details.summary: Cell-free protein synthesis uses extracted cellular machinery to produce proteins in a test tube without living cells. Ribosomes, enzymes, and energy molecules from lysed cells transcribe and translate DNA templates into proteins within hours, bypassing cell growth requirements.

takeaways: Cellular machinery is extracted to produce proteins without intact cells
Proteins are produced in hours instead of the days needed for cell-based methods
Cell-free systems can produce toxic proteins that would kill living cells

faq.question: What are cell-free systems used for in synthetic biology?
faq.answer: Rapid prototyping of genetic circuits before building them in cells, portable point-of-care diagnostics on paper, production of proteins toxic to living hosts, educational kits for teaching, and on-demand manufacturing of therapeutic proteins in resource-limited settings.

faq.question: What are the limitations of cell-free protein synthesis?
faq.answer: Reactions typically last only a few hours before components degrade. They are more expensive per protein molecule than cell-based production. Post-translational modifications like glycosylation are difficult to achieve. Scaling to industrial volumes remains challenging.
